screens.title: Install and Verify Go
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable Go toolchain is the first practical requirement for chaincode development. Installing Go and confirming the runtime version prevents failures during build and test. Start by installing a supported Go release and then run the version command to verify. The purpose of this check is simple: if your compiler or GOPATH is misconfigured, go build and go test will fail with errors that are time-consuming to debug. A concrete example: after installing Go, run the version command in your terminal and confirm it reports a version equal to or newer than the supported baseline. If the version is older, update the runtime rather than trying to patch dependencies. A common misconception is that editor features alone are sufficient; they are helpful, but the underlying compiler and module resolver must function independently of the editor. In practice, when you see dependency errors during go build, re-run the version check and validate your PATH and GOROOT. The key takeaway is: always verify the Go runtime before moving on to editor configuration or module initialization. This habit saves minutes and sometimes hours when you start compiling chaincode.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Install and Verify Go
Definition

Go toolchain verification

Confirm that the installed Go runtime and environment variables are correct so build and test commands succeed reliably.

Command example
# verify installation
go version

# ensure go binaries are in PATH
which go
Explanation & common issues
  • Go must be a supported version for Fabric; mismatched versions can cause build failures.
  • If go is missing from PATH, commands like go build will not run inside terminals launched by editors.
  • Do not assume the editor will install Go for you; the runtime is separate from extensions.
Concrete scenario

After installing Go, run go version. If your CI or container uses a different Go version, align them to avoid subtle build-time mismatches.

Key Takeaway

Always confirm go version and PATH before installing editor tools or initializing modules.

Pro Tip

If your editor shows unresolved imports, check the terminal go version independent of the editor.

Common Mistake

Relying solely on editor notifications without verifying the system go binary leads to confusing errors.

screens.title: Configure VS Code and Go Extension
screens.narratorSegment: Visual Studio Code is the recommended editor for Go chaincode because it provides extensions that deliver intelligence, formatting, and debugging. Start by installing the official Go extension. When you first open a Go file, V S Code will often prompt to install additional language tools such as the Go language server, debugger, and other utilities. Accept those prompts or install them via the command palette. The result is a consistent environment: IntelliSense helps you find contractapi types and methods, formatting keeps code style consistent, and the debugger allows stepping through chaincode logic during unit tests. A common practical workflow is: open the chaincode folder, accept the install tools prompt, then run a quick go build to validate the editor configuration. A misconception to avoid is thinking the extension replaces the Go runtime. It augments your workflow but depends on the underlying go binary and module system. In short: configure both the system Go runtime and the editor tools. That combination gives you fast feedback while writing and testing chaincode. Configure VS Code and Go Extension means use vs code's go extension and install its recommended tools to enable language services, debugging, and formatting for chaincode development.. In practical terms, install the go extension and the recommended go tools for a full development experience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Initialize go.mod and Manage Dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: Go modules are the mechanism that records a project's dependencies and ensures consistent builds. When starting a new chaincode project you must initialize a module in the chaincode root directory. Running the module initialization command creates a go. mod file which is essential for resolving external packages like the Fabric Contract A P I. A concrete walk-through: open the project folder, run the module initialization command with a module path you control, and then run go mod tidy to download and record dependencies. For example, initialize a module named after your repository or a placeholder, and then tidy to add contractapi to go. mod and go. sum. A frequent mistake is to skip go mod init and assume imports will resolve; without a go. mod file go build and go test will fail to find contractapi. Another misconception is that go mod tidy only cleans files — it also downloads required modules. The takeaway: initialize the module early, run go mod tidy after adding imports, and verify the new go. mod contains github. com/hyperledger/fabric-contract-api-go as needed. Initialize go.mod and Manage Dependencies means always run go mod init in your chaincode root and then go mod tidy to fetch contractapi and other dependencies.. In practical terms, use go modules so contractapi and other imports resolve cleanly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Initialize go.mod
Why modules

go.mod defines your module path and records exact dependency versions. For chaincode it ensures contractapi and related packages resolve consistently across machines and CI.

Commands to run
# in your chaincode root directory
go mod init github.com/yourorg/myasset-chaincode
# download and record dependencies
go mod tidy
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting go mod init causes import resolution errors for github.com/hyperledger/fabric-contract-api-go.
  • Using mismatched module paths can cause unexpected import paths in other projects or CI.
  • Not running go mod tidy after editing imports leaves go.sum incomplete and may break reproducible builds.
Concrete check

Inspect go.mod to confirm the module path and that required dependencies are listed after tidy completes.

Key Takeaway

Always initialize a module and run go mod tidy before building chaincode.

Analogy

Think of go.mod as your project's manifest that lists which libraries you rely upon.

Common Mistake

Running go get instead of initializing a module first can leave dependencies unmanaged in modern Go workflows.

screens.title: Fabric Contract API (contractapi)
screens.narratorSegment: The Fabric Contract A P I is a higher-level package that simplifies chaincode development by wrapping common ledger interactions and organizing contract methods as Go struct methods. Instead of directly working with low-level stub calls, you embed the contractapi. Contract into your contract struct and define transaction methods as receiver functions. This structure improves code readability and unit testability by reducing boilerplate. For example, the contractapi's TransactionContextInterface exposes GetStub, so you call GetStub(). PutState rather than calling stub functions directly. A practical benefit is that contractapi handles common concerns like JSON marshaling for assets and passing a transaction context object to each method. A common misconception is that contractapi changes Fabric's endorsement or ordering rules; it does not. It only changes how you structure and implement chaincode logic. The main takeaway: use contractapi for cleaner, maintainable code, and remember system policies like endorsement are still configured at the channel level and enforced independently from your code. Fabric Contract API (contractapi) means embed contractapi.contract to define transaction methods as struct receivers and use transactioncontextinterface for ledger access.. In practical terms, a higher-level programming model for go chaincode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Fabric Contract API
Core idea

A cleaner programming model for chaincode

contractapi provides a higher-level abstraction over the shim so you implement contracts as Go structs with methods representing transactions.

What you get
  • Structured contract types and methods
  • TransactionContextInterface with GetStub convenience
  • Built-in JSON marshaling and utilities
What it doesn't change
  • Endorsement policies and ordering remain configured at the channel level
  • Contract API simplifies code but not network security semantics
Concrete snippet (conceptual)
type MyContract struct {
  contractapi.Contract
}

func (c *MyContract) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, id string, data string) error {
  stub := ctx.GetStub()
  return stub.PutState(id, []byte(data))
}
Key Takeaway

Use contractapi to structure contracts and reduce boilerplate ledger interactions.

Example

Transaction methods receive a context that provides a GetStub helper, improving clarity.

Misconception

contractapi does not change endorsement; it only changes how you write the chaincode logic.

screens.title: TransactionContextInterface and Ledger Access
screens.narratorSegment: When you implement transaction methods with the Fabric Contract A P I you receive a transaction context object. This TransactionContextInterface encapsulates the execution context for a transaction and provides a GetStub method that returns the ledger stub used for state operations. Defining methods this way makes interactions explicit—your method code requests the stub from the context and then calls operations like PutState or GetState. A concrete example: in a CreateAsset method you call ctx. GetStub(). PutState with the asset key and marshaled value. That pattern centralizes access and helps when writing unit tests because you can mock the context or the stub. A common misconception is assuming the context automatically persists changes beyond endorsement; persistence still depends on submitting and committing the transaction. The context only provides controlled access to the stub during transaction execution. The key takeaway is to use TransactionContextInterface consistently so your ledger reads and writes are explicit and testable, and you can more easily inject mocks for unit testing. TransactionContextInterface and Ledger Access means use ctx.getstub() to call putstate and getstate, keeping ledger access explicit and testable.. In practical terms, use the transaction context to interact with the ledger safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › TransactionContextInterface
Definition

TransactionContextInterface carries transaction-scoped data and exposes a GetStub method to retrieve the ledger stub.

func (c *MyContract) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, id string, value string) error {
  stub := ctx.GetStub()
  return stub.PutState(id, []byte(value))
}
Why this helps
  • Explicit stub retrieval clarifies where ledger operations happen.
  • Easy to mock ctx in unit tests to simulate ledger behavior without a network.
  • Reduces boilerplate compared to low-level shim usage.
Misconception

The context does not commit transactions; commit depends on endorsement and ordering configured at the channel level.

Key Takeaway

Use ctx.GetStub() for clear, testable ledger interactions inside transaction methods.

Example

Mock the transaction context in tests to validate method logic without a running peer.

Caution

Do not assume the API persists state; persistence occurs after endorsement and commit phases.

screens.title: Fabric Gateway Client API
screens.narratorSegment: The Fabric Gateway client A P I gives client applications a simplified entry point for submitting transactions and querying the ledger. Instead of manually handling peer discovery, endorsement proposals, and ordering interactions, the Gateway A P I exposes a single gateway connection that routes requests through a Fabric Gateway peer. This abstraction reduces client-side complexity and makes application code easier to write and maintain. A concrete scenario: a web application uses the Gateway A P I to connect to a gateway peer and submit a transaction that invokes your chaincode; the gateway handles discovery and endorsement negotiation. A common misconception is that the Gateway A P I replaces chaincode or network policies; it does not change endorsement, identity, or ordering semantics. The Gateway simply streamlines client interactions. For development, you primarily write and test chaincode, but understanding how the Gateway will call your methods helps you design clear, testable transaction interfaces that client applications can call reliably. Fabric Gateway Client API means use the fabric gateway api from client applications to abstract peer discovery and endorsement, focusing application code on business logic.. In practical terms, how client applications interact with the network in modern fabric versions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Fabric Gateway API

Fabric Gateway client API

A single connection point for client applications to submit transactions and query the ledger while the gateway peer handles discovery and endorsement flow.

Benefits for apps
  • Reduced complexity in client code
  • Automatic endorsement and peer routing by the gateway
  • Cleaner API surface for submitting and evaluating transactions
What remains unchanged
  • Endorsement policies, MSPs, and ordering still govern transaction finality
  • Your chaincode's transaction logic still executes within peer endorsement contexts
Concrete scenario

A backend service uses the Gateway to submit a CreateAsset transaction. The Gateway peer performs discovery and gathers endorsements before the transaction is ordered and committed.

Key Takeaway

Design chaincode methods with clear inputs and outputs so client apps using the Gateway can call them easily.

Example

A REST backend calls the Gateway API to submit transactions rather than orchestrating endorsements itself.

Misconception

The Gateway does not bypass network policies or endorsement rules; it simply centralizes client interactions.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › peer CLI Lifecycle
Typical lifecycle sequence
  1. peer lifecycle chaincode package — bundle source into a package
  2. peer lifecycle chaincode install — place the package on a peer
  3. peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg — approve the definition
  4. peer lifecycle chaincode commit — commit the chaincode to the channel
Ensure the peer binary is available in PATH and that your environment variables point to the correct peer and MSP configuration.
Command examples
# package source
peer lifecycle chaincode package mychaincode.tar.gz --path ./ --lang golang --label mychaincode_1

# install package
peer lifecycle chaincode install mychaincode.tar.gz

# approve definition (example)
peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg --package-id  --sequence 1 --channelID mychannel
Key Takeaway

Practice the package→install→approve→commit loop locally so deployment errors surface early.

Example

Use the output of install to determine the package ID used when approving for your org.

Common Mistake

Not setting peer environment variables results in failed connection attempts when running peer commands.

screens.title: Peer CLI Environment Variables
screens.narratorSegment: The peer CLI depends on environment variables to locate peers and MSP data and to decide whether TLS is enabled. Key variables include CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED which toggles TLS, CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID which identifies the peer's organization MSP, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH that points to the MSP credentials for admin operations, and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS which indicates the peer's network address. If these are incorrect you'll see errors like failed to connect to peer or authentication errors during lifecycle commands. A practical example is when you run install or approve commands: ensure CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH points to an admin's MSP folder; otherwise the peer will reject approval attempts. A common misconception is that a single variable controls everything; in fact multiple variables must be consistent for secure communication. The takeaway: verify each required environment variable and confirm they point to correct certificate paths and addresses before running peer lifecycle commands. This systematic check reduces wasted troubleshooting time during deployment. Peer CLI Environment Variables means core_peer_tls_enabled, core_peer_localmspid, core_peer_mspconfigpath, and core_peer_address must be correctly set to interact with a peer via the cli.. In practical terms, required variables for authentication and peer connectivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Essential variables
CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED — set to true/false to enable TLS
CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID — the peer's organization MSP identifier
CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH — path to admin MSP credentials for signing lifecycle actions

echo $CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH

Consistent and correct peer environment variables are required for successful CLI operations and authentication.

Pro Tip

Validate each variable in the same shell where you run peer commands to avoid context mismatches.

Setting variables in a different shell session or script without exporting them leads to hard-to-diagnose failures.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Environment Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting environment issues is partly about systematic checks and partly about recognizing common root causes. When builds fail, start by confirming the Go version and running go mod tidy to ensure dependencies are fetched. For unresolved imports referencing contractapi, check go. mod and confirm the module path and that tidy completed without errors. If peer CLI commands fail to connect, verify the peer binary is on PATH and inspect CORE_PEER_ADDRESS and CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH. When V S Code shows unresolved symbols but the terminal go build succeeds, check that the editor is using the same Go binary and that recommended Go tools are installed. A concrete debugging sequence is: run go build in the terminal, run go mod tidy, echo peer env variables, and try an install command while watching error messages for missing file paths or TLS issues. A common misdiagnosis is assuming the network or Fabric binaries are at fault when the real problem is a missing or incorrect go. mod. The takeaway: follow a short checklist—runtime, modules, editor tools, peer env—so you can isolate and fix the issue quickly.

Run build and tests from the same terminal you use for peer commands to ensure consistent environment variables.

Assuming network components are failing before checking local module and runtime settings wastes time.

screens.title: Development Workflow and Local Testing

Start by writing and unit-testing your chaincode functions locally using the Go testing framework and by mocking the TransactionContextInterface when appropriate. Once unit tests pass, build the chaincode binary to validate compilation. Next, package the source using the peer lifecycle package command and install it on a local peer. A common misconception is to skip unit tests and rely only on integration tests; unit tests catch logic errors faster and are easier to run frequently. The takeaway: combine unit tests, editor debugging, and local lifecycle deployment so you validate both code correctness and integration with the Fabric runtime before pushing to broader test networks. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Development Workflow
Workflow steps
1. Write contract methods and tests
2. Run unit tests with mocked context
3. Build and package with peer lifecycle
4. Install, approve, commit, and run integration tests
This sequence ensures you validate logic in isolation and then confirm behavior inside a full node environment accessed by client apps via the Gateway API.
Concrete test example

Create a unit test that injects a fake stub into your contract method to assert state changes, then run go test. After packaging and installing, run an integration call through the Gateway to confirm end-to-end behavior.

Why both matter
  • Unit tests catch logic bugs quickly and are fast to run.
  • Integration tests validate configuration, endorsement, and commit flows.
Key Takeaway

Iterate locally with tests and the peer lifecycle so you detect issues early and deliver reliable chaincode.

Pro Tip

Mock the transaction context in unit tests and keep integration tests for end-to-end validation.

Common Mistake

Relying only on integration tests slows the cycle and obscures whether failures are logic bugs or deployment issues.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we set up a dependable environment for writing chaincode in Go and learn the tools that make development productive and testable. You will verify a Go installation, configure Visual Studio Code with the Go extension and language tools, and initialize your project with a Go module so dependencies resolve cleanly. We also introduce the Fabric Contract A P I, which gives you a higher-level programming model to structure smart contracts, and the Fabric Gateway client A P I, which your applications will use to talk to the network. During development you'll use the peer CLI to package, install, approve, and commit your chaincode; we'll highlight the environment variables that enable those commands to authenticate and connect. A solid setup reduces build errors, prevents dependency headaches, and speeds iteration when you run tests and package chaincode for a local network. As you move through the chapter, notice the concrete commands and typical mistakes so you can avoid wasted time later. By the end you'll be able to boot your editor, initialize a Go module, and perform basic lifecycle steps confidently.

In this section we'll make explicit the practical skills you will gain so you can check progress as you work. First, you'll learn how to set up a Go-based development environment and verify the Go toolchain is functioning. This matters because a broken compiler or missing tools stops you before you write any code. Second, you'll identify and configure V S Code and the Go extension along with the language tools V S Code recommends. That setup enables IntelliSense, debugging, and automated formatting which reduce errors and speed development. Third, you'll understand the Fabric Contract A P I and the Fabric Gateway client A P I so you can design chaincode methods cleanly and know how clients will invoke them. Finally, you'll use the peer CLI for packaging, installing, approving, and committing chaincode during development, and you will troubleshoot common environment issues like incorrect go. mod or misconfigured peer environment variables. Each objective focuses on a practical competency: install, configure, implement, and debug. By the end you should be able to initialize a module, run go mod tidy, accept V S Code tool installs, and perform basic lifecycle steps with the peer CLI.

This second objectives slide highlights the practical outcomes you will exercise during a hands-on setup. You will initialize a Go module and run go mod tidy to fetch contractapi dependencies so builds succeed. You will accept and run the additional Go tools that V S Code prompts for; those tools provide features like language server support and an integrated debugger which make stepping through chaincode logic possible. You'll also perform peer lifecycle commands to package, install, approve, and commit chaincode on a development peer; learning these steps is vital because packaging mistakes or missing approvals are common causes of deployment failure. Finally, you'll practice checking and correcting peer-related environment variables such as TLS settings and MSP paths. Each of these outcomes maps directly to a testable action: verify go version, initialize go. mod, run go mod tidy, install Go tools, and successfully run a peer lifecycle package and install. These are the tasks you will repeat during iterative development and integration testing.

A reliable Go toolchain is the first practical requirement for chaincode development. Installing Go and confirming the runtime version prevents failures during build and test. Start by installing a supported Go release and then run the version command to verify. The purpose of this check is simple: if your compiler or GOPATH is misconfigured, go build and go test will fail with errors that are time-consuming to debug. A concrete example: after installing Go, run the version command in your terminal and confirm it reports a version equal to or newer than the supported baseline. If the version is older, update the runtime rather than trying to patch dependencies. A common misconception is that editor features alone are sufficient; they are helpful, but the underlying compiler and module resolver must function independently of the editor. In practice, when you see dependency errors during go build, re-run the version check and validate your PATH and GOROOT. The key takeaway is: always verify the Go runtime before moving on to editor configuration or module initialization. This habit saves minutes and sometimes hours when you start compiling chaincode.

Visual Studio Code is the recommended editor for Go chaincode because it provides extensions that deliver intelligence, formatting, and debugging. Start by installing the official Go extension. When you first open a Go file, V S Code will often prompt to install additional language tools such as the Go language server, debugger, and other utilities. Accept those prompts or install them via the command palette. The result is a consistent environment: IntelliSense helps you find contractapi types and methods, formatting keeps code style consistent, and the debugger allows stepping through chaincode logic during unit tests. A common practical workflow is: open the chaincode folder, accept the install tools prompt, then run a quick go build to validate the editor configuration. A misconception to avoid is thinking the extension replaces the Go runtime. It augments your workflow but depends on the underlying go binary and module system. In short: configure both the system Go runtime and the editor tools. That combination gives you fast feedback while writing and testing chaincode. Configure VS Code and Go Extension means use vs code's go extension and install its recommended tools to enable language services, debugging, and formatting for chaincode development.. In practical terms, install the go extension and the recommended go tools for a full development experience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Go modules are the mechanism that records a project's dependencies and ensures consistent builds. When starting a new chaincode project you must initialize a module in the chaincode root directory. Running the module initialization command creates a go. mod file which is essential for resolving external packages like the Fabric Contract A P I. A concrete walk-through: open the project folder, run the module initialization command with a module path you control, and then run go mod tidy to download and record dependencies. For example, initialize a module named after your repository or a placeholder, and then tidy to add contractapi to go. mod and go. sum. A frequent mistake is to skip go mod init and assume imports will resolve; without a go. mod file go build and go test will fail to find contractapi. Another misconception is that go mod tidy only cleans files — it also downloads required modules. The takeaway: initialize the module early, run go mod tidy after adding imports, and verify the new go. mod contains github. com/hyperledger/fabric-contract-api-go as needed. Initialize go.mod and Manage Dependencies means always run go mod init in your chaincode root and then go mod tidy to fetch contractapi and other dependencies.. In practical terms, use go modules so contractapi and other imports resolve cleanly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Fabric Contract A P I is a higher-level package that simplifies chaincode development by wrapping common ledger interactions and organizing contract methods as Go struct methods. Instead of directly working with low-level stub calls, you embed the contractapi. Contract into your contract struct and define transaction methods as receiver functions. This structure improves code readability and unit testability by reducing boilerplate. For example, the contractapi's TransactionContextInterface exposes GetStub, so you call GetStub(). PutState rather than calling stub functions directly. A practical benefit is that contractapi handles common concerns like JSON marshaling for assets and passing a transaction context object to each method. A common misconception is that contractapi changes Fabric's endorsement or ordering rules; it does not. It only changes how you structure and implement chaincode logic. The main takeaway: use contractapi for cleaner, maintainable code, and remember system policies like endorsement are still configured at the channel level and enforced independently from your code. Fabric Contract API (contractapi) means embed contractapi.contract to define transaction methods as struct receivers and use transactioncontextinterface for ledger access.. In practical terms, a higher-level programming model for go chaincode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you implement transaction methods with the Fabric Contract A P I you receive a transaction context object. This TransactionContextInterface encapsulates the execution context for a transaction and provides a GetStub method that returns the ledger stub used for state operations. Defining methods this way makes interactions explicit—your method code requests the stub from the context and then calls operations like PutState or GetState. A concrete example: in a CreateAsset method you call ctx. GetStub(). PutState with the asset key and marshaled value. That pattern centralizes access and helps when writing unit tests because you can mock the context or the stub. A common misconception is assuming the context automatically persists changes beyond endorsement; persistence still depends on submitting and committing the transaction. The context only provides controlled access to the stub during transaction execution. The key takeaway is to use TransactionContextInterface consistently so your ledger reads and writes are explicit and testable, and you can more easily inject mocks for unit testing. TransactionContextInterface and Ledger Access means use ctx.getstub() to call putstate and getstate, keeping ledger access explicit and testable.. In practical terms, use the transaction context to interact with the ledger safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down.
